newsitem.title: USA: Robust U.S. economy arouses consumer confidence.
newsitem.headline: Robust U.S. economy arouses consumer confidence.

text.p: The resilient U.S. economy has American consumers feeling almost as confident as they did in the summer of 1969.
Consumer confidence in the economy in June was the highest since August 1969, the Conference Board said on Tuesday.
The private business research group reported that its index of U.S. consumer confidence rose to 129.6 for the month, nearing the 131.7 reading 28 years ago.
Consumer confidence generally reflects longer-term attitudes and longer-term economic conditions, noted Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
Cruising into its seventh year of expansion, the U.S. economy continues to ride the wave of low unemployment, low inflation and steady interest rates.
That economic environment puts the average consumer in a comfort zone, said Kretzmer.

"It just reflects the stability of the current environment, the maintenance of low inflation, the low unemployment and the absence of a recession," Kretzmer said. "(It) just makes poeple feel much more comfortable."

Consumer confidence increased this month in seven of America's nine major regions, with the greatest gains coming from the Middle Atlantic and Pacific regions, according to the Conference Board's survey of 5,000 U.S. households.

In addition, some 36 percent of all consumers say buisness conditions are "good," up from about 33 percent in May, the survey showed. Nearly 36 percent said jobs were plentiful, up from about 35 percent in May, it said.
"Overall, the economy is doing quite well ... and there seems to be no signs of a let up in growth," said Lynn Franco, associate director of The Conference Board's Consumer Research Center.

"Consumers feel that conditions today are healthier than they were a year ago, and certainly there is nothing really coming out of any other sectors that ... signal a severe sudden downturn in confidence levels or the pace of activity."
The University also measures U.S. consumer attitudes, in bi-monthly consumer sentiment survey that has been issued regularly since the late 1970s.

For the past several releases, that index has set a series of all-time record highs. It currently stands at 103.4 in the preliminary June report. The final reading for the month will be issued on June 27.
Still, despite high confidence levels and plentiful jobs, U.S. consumers do not appear to be spending much on cars, homes and major appliances.
Consumers' plans to buy those types of goods within the next six months declined in June versus May, the Conference Board survey said.
Paul Kasriel, chief economist at Northern Trust Co in Chicago, said that if consumer confidence continues to surge, a rebound in consumer spending may be nearing.
"It suggests that one of these days consumers are going to start buying again," he said.
